parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**Vegetable Palace (VP) **

VP was started 10 years ago in country Z. It is a public limited company. VP has a chain of 500 fast-food restaurants that operate across country Z. The VP brand is famous for its vegetarian food, this means none of its meals contain meat.

VP has a head office in Main City where all the directors and senior managers work. There are many barriers to communication. Each VP restaurant has a Manager, an Assistant Manager and 50 employees who cook and serve the meals. Restaurant Managers are often very busy and they are considering delegating some of their tasks to the Assistant Managers.

The ingredients for the restaurants are ordered in bulk by head office and then distributed from its warehouse to each of the restaurants. However, some senior managers think that Restaurant Managers should purchase their own ingredients from local suppliers. This would mean the ingredients would be fresher and would allow variations in the meals served.

VP wants to expand into another country. It will choose between the two countries shown in Appendix 2. VP will also need to decide how to enter a new market in another country. It has the option of forming a joint venture with another business or franchising the VP brand. The choice of finance will need to be considered for the expansion and the amount of finance will depend on the option chosen.

**Appendix 1 **

**Advertisement for VP's restaurants **

Choose VP for the finest vegetarian meals. Our service is the fastest possible!

You will receive your meal in less than 5 minutes – guaranteed!

Delicious and varied meals for even the biggest of appetites and all at competitive prices.

New meals are being introduced all the time.

There is a VP restaurant near you – we look forward to serving you soon.

**Appendix 2 **

**Summary of the two possible countries that VP could choose to locate its new restaurants.**

|   | **Country A** | **Country B** |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw materials** | Average variable cost \$6 per meal | Average variable cost \$2 per meal |
| **Labour** | Low unemployment \$10 per hour for each employee | High unemployment \$5 per hour for each employee |
| **Market** | Many competitors Average price per meal = \$20 | Few competitors Average price per meal = \$10 |

**Appendix 3 **

**Email from VP’s Managing Director to VP’s Marketing Director **

To: VP’s Marketing Director

From: VP’s Managing Director

Date: 31 March 2023

Re: Economic changes in country Z

Did you see the news this morning that interest rates will be raised from 3% to 5% later today? This will have several effects on our business in country Z.

The news also said that the exchange rate in country Z has depreciated. We will have to consider how this will affect our business, especially as we import 30% of our ingredients into country Z.

There are also new legal controls being introduced that mean we have to list all the ingredients used in each of our meals on the menu. We do reprint menus every time we change the meals, but it is something to consider.

Speak later today.

Consider the benefits and limitations of the following **two** ways VP can respond to pressure from health and environmental groups when entering a new market in another country.

- Adapting the menu to meet health and environmental standards demanded by pressure groups
- Maintaining current menu offerings to preserve profitability

Which approach should VP choose? **Justify** your answer.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2023-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf) when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
Adapting the menu to meet health and environmental standards would help VP build a positive reputation with pressure groups, which could lead to endorsements and positive publicity **[An]**. For example, VP might introduce more organic ingredients or reduce packaging waste to satisfy environmental campaigners **[Ap]**. This could attract health-conscious customers and improve brand image **[An]**

However, adapting the menu could significantly increase costs through sourcing premium ingredients and changing suppliers **[An]**. VP might need to pay higher prices for organic vegetables **[Ap]** or sustainable packaging, reducing profit margins **[An]**

Maintaining current menu offerings would preserve VP's established profit margins and keep costs low **[An]**. This approach would allow VP to offer competitive prices, particularly important if entering Country A where average meal prices are lower **[Ap]**, helping to attract price-sensitive customers **[An]**

However, ignoring pressure groups could result in negative publicity campaigns and boycotts **[An]**, such as protests outside VP restaurants highlighting unhealthy ingredients **[Ap]**. This could damage brand reputation and reduce customer loyalty **[An]**

VP should adapt its menu to meet health and environmental standards **[E]**. This approach aligns with growing consumer awareness about health and sustainability issues **[Ap]**. Meeting pressure group demands would differentiate VP from competitors and create long-term customer loyalty **[E]**. The initial cost increases would be offset by premium pricing opportunities and increased market share **[E]**. Unlike maintaining current offerings, adapting the menu positions VP as a responsible business, essential for sustainable growth in international markets **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the approach
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
>   - Add a final Evaluation (E):
>   
>     - Decide which approach is most beneficial/problematic
>     - Justify your choice
>     - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Adapting menu to meet standards**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Positive publicity from pressure groups → enhanced brand reputation → increased customer loyalty
>     - Attracts health-conscious consumers → access to premium market segments → higher sales potential
>     - Avoids boycotts and protests → maintains stable operations → protects revenue streams
>     - Demonstrates corporate social responsibility → improves stakeholder relationships → long-term sustainability
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Higher ingredient costs → organic and sustainable sourcing → reduced profit margins
>     - Supply chain complexity → finding certified suppliers → increased operational costs
>     - Menu development costs → research and testing → additional investment required
>     - Price increases may deter customers → reduced competitiveness → potential market share loss
> - **Maintaining current offerings**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Preserves established profit margins → lower costs → maintains financial performance
>     - Competitive pricing strategy → attracts price-sensitive customers → market penetration
>     - No supply chain disruption → operational efficiency → consistent service delivery
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Negative publicity campaigns → boycotts and protests → damaged brand reputation
>     - Loss of health-conscious customers → reduced market appeal → limited growth potential
>     - Regulatory pressure → potential future compliance costs → operational risks
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Adapting menu: builds positive reputation and attracts conscious consumers → good for long-term growth, but increases costs and complexity.
>   - Maintaining offerings: preserves profitability and operational simplicity → but risks reputation damage and market limitations.
>   - VP should choose the approach that best balances stakeholder demands with sustainable profitability

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**RMT Clothing Ltd**

RMT Clothing Ltd is a medium-sized clothing retailer based in Country X. It was founded in 1995 and has grown to 50 stores across the country, selling affordable fashion for men and women aged 18-35. RMT currently employs 800 people, and had annual revenue of \$85 million last year.

The company is facing increasing competition from online retailers. RMT's CEO, Sarah Jones, is considering whether to close 10 underperforming stores and invest in expanding the company's e-commerce operations instead. This would involve making 100 store staff redundant but hiring 50 new employees to work on the website and in the distribution centre.

RMT's financial performance over the last 3 years is shown in table 1 below.

**Table 1: RMT’s Financial Performance 2020 to 2022**

| Year | Revenue (\$m) | Profit (\$m) | Online sales (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 80 | 4.0 | 15 |
| 2021 | 82 | 3.8 | 18 |
| 2022 | 85 | 3.5 | 22 |

The company's main stakeholders have differing views on the proposed changes. Shareholders are concerned about falling profits and want to see a clear plan for growth. Employees are worried about potential job losses. Customers have been complaining that RMT's website is difficult to use compared to competitors.

RMT is also facing external challenges including rising energy and material costs, as well as changing consumer preferences towards more sustainable fashion. However, there are opportunities to expand into new international markets through e-commerce.

Sarah needs to decide on the best strategy to ensure RMT's long-term success in a rapidly changing retail environment.

Consider the potential responses of the following two pressure groups to RMT's proposed changes:

- Trade unions representing retail workers
- Local community groups in areas where stores may close

Analyse how each pressure group might respond to RMT's plans for redundancies and store closures. Which pressure group should RMT be most concerned about? **Justify** your answer.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/rmt-clothing-ltd-case-study.pdf) when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
Trade unions would likely oppose the redundancies strongly **[Ap]**, as protecting jobs is their primary purpose and 100 workers would lose employment **[An]**. They could organise strikes or industrial action to disrupt RMT's operations **[An]**, potentially damaging productivity and customer service during the transition period **[An]**. Trade unions might also launch negative publicity campaigns highlighting job losses **[Ap]**, which could harm RMT's brand reputation and customer loyalty **[An]**. However, unions might be willing to negotiate if RMT offers retraining for the 50 new e-commerce roles **[An]**.

Local community groups would be concerned about losing retail services in their areas **[Ap]**, as store closures reduce shopping convenience for residents **[An]**. They could organise boycotts of remaining RMT stores **[An]**, encouraging local customers to shop with competitors instead **[An]**. Community groups might lobby local councils to refuse planning permission for future RMT developments **[Ap]**, limiting the company's expansion opportunities **[An]**. However, their influence may be limited to specific geographical areas **[An]**.

I recommend RMT should be most concerned about trade unions **[E]**. While community groups affect local areas, trade unions have national influence and can disrupt operations across all RMT stores through coordinated action **[E]**. The timing is critical as RMT needs smooth operations during the transition to e-commerce **[Ap]**, and industrial action could delay the restructuring and worsen financial performance **[E]**. Trade unions also have stronger legal protections and established negotiation processes **[E]**, making them harder to ignore than community pressure groups **[E]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each pressure group identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the pressure group's main concern
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail about redundancies/closures
>   - Analysis (An): Explain potential responses and business impact
>   - Add a final Evaluation (E):
>   
>     - Decide which pressure group poses the greatest threat
>     - Justify your choice with business reasoning
>     - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts about job losses and store closures
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms for pressure group responses
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Trade unions representing retail workers**
> 
>   - **Potential responses**
>   
>     - Organise strikes and industrial action → disrupts operations and customer service
>     - Launch publicity campaigns against job losses → damages brand reputation
>     - Negotiate for better redundancy packages → increases restructuring costs
>     - Demand retraining opportunities for affected workers → may delay implementation
>   - **Concerns and impact**
>   
>     - 100 redundancies directly affect union members → strong motivation to resist
>     - National reach allows coordinated action across multiple stores → widespread disruption
>     - Legal rights to collective bargaining → cannot be easily dismissed
>     - Media support for workers' rights → amplifies negative publicity
> - **Local community groups**
> 
>   - **Potential responses**
>   
>     - Organise local boycotts of RMT stores → reduces sales in affected areas
>     - Lobby councils against future planning applications → limits expansion opportunities
>     - Campaign for alternative retailers to fill vacant premises → increases local competition
>     - Generate negative local media coverage → damages community relations
>   - **Concerns and impact**
>   
>     - Loss of local shopping convenience → affects community cohesion
>     - Reduced footfall in local shopping areas → impacts other businesses
>     - Limited to specific geographical areas → localised rather than national impact
>     - Less formal organisation → easier for RMT to manage individually
> - **Recommendation**
> 
>   - Trade unions pose the greater threat because they can coordinate national action affecting all RMT operations, not just closed stores
>   - Their legal rights and established negotiation processes make them harder to ignore than community groups
>   - Industrial action during the critical transition period could severely damage RMT's restructuring plans and financial recovery

parts.problem_md: Do you think all businesses suffer when they come under the scrutiny of pressure groups? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Pressure groups can damage a business's reputation through negative publicity **[K]**. This could lead to a fall in sales as consumers may boycott the business's products **[An]**

However, pressure group scrutiny can force businesses to improve their practices **[K]**. This can lead to better corporate social responsibility which may attract more customers and improve long-term profitability **[An]**

Overall, I think not all businesses suffer from pressure group scrutiny. For example, if environmental pressure groups target a business for poor sustainability practices, this may initially damage sales **[E]**. However, if the business responds by adopting greener practices, it can attract environmentally conscious consumers and gain a competitive advantage over rivals who have not made these changes **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason affects the business (cause-effect chain) → 1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also affect the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Increased costs of compliance [k] reducing profit margins [an]
>   - Forced to change practices [k] which can improve corporate image [an] and attract ethical consumers [an]
>   - Can highlight issues early [k] allowing businesses to address problems before they become serious [an]
>   - May face legal action/fines [k] increasing costs and damaging finances [an]
>   - Can create competitive advantage [k] if business responds better than competitors [an]
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - Pressure groups can damage reputation through negative publicity [k].
>   - However, scrutiny can force businesses to improve practices [k] leading to better corporate social responsibility which attracts customers [an].
>   - Overall, not all businesses suffer. For example, environmental pressure groups may initially damage sales, but if businesses adopt greener practices, they can attract environmentally conscious consumers and gain competitive advantage over rivals. [eval]

parts.problem_md: Do you think businesses are more affected by pressure groups than by other stakeholder groups? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Businesses may be more affected by other stakeholder groups because shareholders have direct financial control over company decisions **[K]**. This gives them immediate power to influence strategic direction and operational priorities through voting rights and investment decisions **[An]**

However, pressure groups can mobilise widespread public campaigns and coordinate boycotts that significantly impact sales revenue **[K]**, as they can reach large consumer bases and create sustained negative publicity that damages brand reputation **[An]**

Businesses should recognise that whilst shareholders and employees have direct contractual relationships that create immediate operational pressures, pressure groups often represent broader societal concerns that can lead to regulatory changes and long-term market shifts **[E]**. Furthermore, companies that prioritise shareholder demands over pressure group concerns may achieve short-term financial gains but risk facing coordinated activism that can ultimately threaten their social licence to operate and sustainable profitability **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason affects the business (cause-effect chain) → 1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also affect the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which stakeholder group has greater impact overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Shareholders control investment and dividend decisions [k] directly affecting company financing and strategic options [an]
>   - Employees can strike or reduce productivity [k] immediately disrupting operations and profitability [an]
>   - Customers make direct purchasing decisions [k] providing immediate revenue feedback on business actions [an]
>   - Pressure groups lack direct financial control [k] limiting their immediate operational impact [an]
>   - Pressure groups can coordinate large-scale campaigns [k] creating widespread reputational damage and consumer boycotts [an]
>   - Pressure groups influence government policy [k] leading to regulatory changes that affect entire industries [an]
>   - Other stakeholders have contractual relationships [k] giving them legal rights and immediate influence [an]
> 
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - Yes, pressure groups have greater impact as they can mobilise public opinion [k] creating market-wide changes that affect long-term sustainability [an].
>   - No, other stakeholder groups like shareholders and employees have direct control mechanisms [k] that immediately affect business operations and decision-making [an].
>   - Other stakeholder groups have greater immediate impact through direct financial and operational control, but pressure groups create longer-term systemic risks that can fundamentally threaten business models and market position. [eval] [eval]

parts.problem_md: Do you think businesses should always respond to the actions of pressure groups? **Justify** your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Businesses may choose not to always respond to pressure groups because responding to every campaign can be extremely costly **[K]**. This diverts resources from core business operations and may reduce profitability and competitiveness **[An]**

However, businesses that ignore legitimate pressure group concerns risk facing organised boycotts and negative publicity campaigns **[K]**, as these groups can mobilise public opinion and damage brand reputation significantly **[An]**

Businesses should consider that whilst ignoring pressure groups may preserve short-term operational efficiency, failing to address valid concerns can result in regulatory intervention and loss of social licence to operate **[E]**. Furthermore, companies that engage constructively with pressure groups often identify emerging social issues early and can adapt their practices proactively, ultimately building stronger stakeholder relationships and sustainable competitive advantage **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) → 1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Shareholders expect focus on core business activities [k] so responding to all campaigns may distract management [an]
>   - Some pressure group demands may conflict with business objectives [k] creating operational difficulties [an]
>   - Constant policy changes to satisfy groups [k] can confuse customers and employees [an]
>   - Pressure groups represent important stakeholder views [k] which can influence consumer purchasing decisions [an]
>   - Early engagement helps identify emerging issues [k] allowing proactive rather than reactive responses [an]
>   - Strong stakeholder relationships improve corporate reputation [k] attracting socially conscious consumers and investors [an]
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - No, businesses cannot respond to every pressure group as this would be financially unsustainable [k] and may compromise core business operations [an].
>   - However, ignoring all pressure group concerns damages stakeholder relationships [k] leading to reputational damage and potential regulatory intervention [an].
>   - Businesses should selectively respond to legitimate pressure group concerns that align with stakeholder interests and business values, as this balances operational efficiency with social responsibility. [eval] [eval]
